HAMBURGH, April 9. The Hanover Gazette publishes the answer which the Curatorium of the University made on the 22d of November. 837, to th seven professors on the subject of their remonstrance of the 18th of the same month. The Guratorium appreciates the frankness with which the professors have communicated their doubts respecting the roval patent of the 1st of the month, and acknowledges that different opinions may be entertained on so important a matter, and the King had accordingly not taken his resolution without mature consideration. The Curatorium declines entering into a discussion of bis Majesty's motives or of the principles laid down by the professors, and cannot allow that persons in office or private individuals have any right to subject measures which proceed from the Sovereign to discussion, as it were to treat with him and to refuse obedience to his royal decrees. It is rather the duty of subjects to wait calmly till the public concerns of the country shall be regulated in the only legal way, viz. by deliberations in the Estates winch are convoked, but it cannot be allowed that every one should act after his own individual opinion, which would manifestly lead

to anarchy. If they were confined to observe the constitution, they received this injunction from their lawful Sovereign, to whom alone the oath of persons in office is taken ; it is now revoked in the same manner by the legitimate Sovereign, and the public servant must obey this new order, since the Sovereign cannot allow a person in office to renounce his obedience and to declare that he will act directly against Ins declared will. The Curatorium is convinced that this is the prevailing opinion of all persons in office, and the more so as the seven professors were the first and only persons who have made a similar declaration. It can surely not be assumed that these officers have not acted conscientiously, and the professors doubtless did not mean to say so in the very extraordinary expression they have employed at the conclusion of their representation. The Curatorium, instead of immediately submitting this address to the King, will rather consider it as a confidential communication, and wishes the professors deliberately to consider what has

IDASTSS T33!P3Sra&233L been just said, and to reflect on the danger to which by such a declaration they expose themselves, their official situations, and even the property of the University itself, and hopes they will submit to the patent; and when ihe University shall be called upon to choose a representative, will make no opposition, since it is of the highest importance to ihe count r\ that the question of the future constitution, which is to be laid before the Estates, shall he calmly considered and settled to the advantage of the kingdom and the country, it being, of course, understood, that if any one of them lie elected, he is free to refuse, which he may the rather do, as the long absence that would ensue wouid not be compatible with their official duties. The Curato rium expects that they will be very careful in their language on this important subject, and avoid whatever may inflame the young men, and lead them to take steps injurious to themselves and probably to tiie whole University The King has been pleased to consent to an adjournment of l tie? The most extensive preparations on a seal of surpassing grandeur have commenced at Goldsmith' Hall in the Gity, for the entertainment of the -Queen, who has most graciously consented to accept the invitation of this, the richest company in the world. From the Q,nehec Met "ury. June 23. þÿ Lieut. Colonel the Hon. C Grey arrived yesterday by the steamer from Montreal, bearing despatches for the Governor General from Mr Fox, her Majesty's minister to the United States. We understand that Colonel Grey had several interviews with the President and Secretary of War, Mr. Poinsett, all of which were highly satisfactory, and indicative of the firm determination of the United States Government to co operate with the Governor General in putting down the disgraceful disturbances which have taken place upon the frontiers. Gen. Macomb, the commander-in-chief of the United States army, has taken the command on the frontier, and his orders from the Secretary of War are, to co operate with our naval and military authoritics in any way that may be considered most effectual."

From Canada. þÿ Accounts have been received this morning from Canada of the entire deleat of the insurgent force in the neighborhood of the Short Hills yesterday, and the capture of their standards arid ringleaders. A large body of troops, and tiOO Indian warriors, had been previously collected in their rear, and gradually hemmed them in. It is said that there are many Americans among the prisoners, who will most probably be tried by a Field Court Martial, and be executed forthwith. All communication across the river has been suspended, and the boats drawn lip to prevent the escape of any parties still lurking in the woods. From the Buffalo Commercial Advertiser, June 27. We learn this afternoon by a gentleman from Waterloo, that every thing is perfectly quit on that side of the lines the ferries are þÿ running as usual, and persons can pass freely back and forth, with but slight examination, piovided no suspicious appearances exist. It is presumed that ail restriction will he shortly removed, nothing it unusual occurs. The statement published by us that the insurgents at Short Hills had been captured and dispersed, is confirmed. Some 20, all Canadians- were taken in the immediate vicinity of the outbreak, and a number more have been subsequently taken on Cull Island, at the mouth of Grand Kiver. These were nearly all Americans, and a physician from this side, whose name we do not learn, was among them. The Tamarack Swamp, extending; from Short Hills to Grand River,

which was the retreat of the insurgents, has been pretty thoroughly cleared. The prisoners captured have b en taken to Chippewa, for trial, before a commission. The Attorney General is in readiness, and the proceedings will probably be had to-dnv or to morrow. The punishment of those from this side, who may tie declared guilty, will, we suppose, be death. Gov. Arthur was at Chippewa, dav before yesterday, and left in the evening for Toronto, From the Buflalo Journal, June 20. We learn that Me Lend, and a number of others, concerned in the Short Hills atfiiir, have been captured, and the remainder of the antirovalist party dispersed. Intercourse between the two territories seems, for the present, to be stopped at þÿ least so far as concerns the action of the Canadian authorities. A number ot persons who crossed at the Falls yesterday, for the purpose of viewing the natural curiosities, were at once marshalled before the military authorities to give an account of themselves, and were then immediately ordered back to the American side. There is a great deal of folly in this excess of prudence, and we hope it will be suffered to blow over in a few days.
The British fleet now on the North American station is composed of 32 vessels, and carries 1100 guns, and 10,210 men.

From the Old Quebec Gazette. His Excellency the Governor General will leave Quebec on Wednesday the 4th July, in the John Bull steamer upon the tour of inspection which it is his intention to take throughout the two Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada As it is the Noble Earl's intention to visit tne defences upon the whole of our frontier line, he will be accompanied by Sir Charles Paget, the Vice Admiral upon the station, and Sir John Colborne, Commander of the Forces. Sir Charles Paget will proceed tomorrow in H. M. S. Medea to Montreal, where he will await the arrival of the Earl of Durham. His Excellency will remain, it is understood, three or four days in Montreal. He will then proceed at once to Kingston, U. C. thence to Toronto, minute- ' ly inspecting the defences naval as well as military, by the way. Upon his return His Excellency will probably deviate materially from the direct course to visit such portions of the Provinces as may seem to require his presence.

THE þÿCROPS THE HARVEST. An all bountiful Providence has not only blessed our country with abundant crops, but also with the most favorable season for their in-gathering. We never recollect to have witnessed a more genial period for the growth and final ripening of the crops than the last six or eight weeks have presented, or a more advantageous condition of the weather since the harvest has commenced. Each day's continuance of such weather as we have had for the eight or ten just past, secures to the country hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat.

Talleyrand and Cobbett. þÿ A Philadelphia Correspondent of Mc'Kenzie's Gazette, says that in 1795 William Cobbett, then in Philadelphia, taught Talleyrand, Volney, a then exiled mayor of Paris and other French exiles, the English language. Cobbett then wrote a book to enable Frenchmen to speak and read English, which is to this day used in Paris. He was very poor. His parlour' kitchen, and bedrooms scarcely occupied the space taken up by an ordinary sitting room. Afterwards lie took to writing political j pamphlets, opened shop for himself, and be- j came notorious as a party politician Thomas | Paine was employed, by the Whigs to write Common Sense and the Crisis. Sydney on Government was placed in his hands, and he gave it a modern dress. O, but he liked a glass of bitters well I When in prison, he wrote bis Age of Reason to please Robespierre and got out. þÿ He would not have ( done so but for the dangerous situation in which he was placed.

The Prince de Joinville, with his suit arrived in town by the Providence Railroad cars yesterday morning The Prince, very discreetly, on the arrival of tbe train at the depot, immediately left the car, and with a friend proceeded on foot across the common, in cog, to the Tremont House, and thus avoided the curious multitude who were waiting to see him enter his carriage. He made a hasty visit to the Navy Yard & a few other public objects, and in the afternoon sat out on his return to Newport. A splendid entertainment was given to the Prince, at the Astor House, iu New York, by the French residents, on Saturday evening.

The Mails pr: first July packet from England reached this Island on Sunday. The papers are full of details of the ceremonies, and processions attending the coronation of Her Majesty Victoria 1st Queen of Great Britain. The coronation took place on the 28th of June þÿ the weather which commenced with showers till 8 o'clock in the morning, O7 then cleared up, and a brilliant sun shine succeeded. The procession moved front Buckingham Palace at ten o'clock. The carriages of the Foreign Ambassadors taking the lead. Then followed the different members of the 1 toy a I Family, þÿ afterwards the Queen's carriages, Twelve of which, each drawn by six nurses, preceeded Her Majesty, who was in her state carriage drawn by eight cteani colored horses, þÿ those ot the Foreinu Amoassadors were drawn by two horses each. Squadrons of Life Guards, Hussars and Lancers, accompanied the procession, þÿ the Queen appeared excellent spirits, and was in most enthusiastically ciiceied the whole distance from the palace to Westminster Abbev, which the procession reached at eleven o'clock This extensive and venerable structure, had been most superbly fitted up lor the occasion þÿ galleries had been erected extending nearly to the ceiling, (over 100 feet iri height), to accommodate the brilliant assemblage within its walls, þÿ a choir of 500 musicians occupied a superb orchestra þÿ and the whole had the appearance of a magnificent theatre Idled with England's Nobility, Foreign Ambassadors with their Suites, Stran-

gers of distinction, and a most brilliant display of Englands beauty, sparkling with dia nionds, and arrayed in the richest costumes, the whole effect was to strike Strangers with admiration at the riches and power of Great Britain. All the ancient ceremonies at Coronations were observed. The administering the oath, anointing with holy oil, the crowning hv the Archbishop Canterbury, of the Queen kneeling on this and other occasions, the homage and fealty made to her Majesty by the other branches of the Royal Family, and by the Bishops and Peers, the Sermon preached by the Bishop of London, the To Ileum's and Anthem's performed in great stile by the immense choir, were all gone through, and occupied the time till four o'clock. The Queen bore the ceremony well, and altho' signs of fatigue were observable at its close, yet Her Majesty appeared so gratified with the strong marks of attachment universally displayed towards her, and more particularly as she returned crowned to Buckingham palace, as to entirely overcome the effect of the exertions and feelings called into action on the occasion. þÿ Marshal Sonlt wherever recognized, was most cordially greeted bv the assembled multitudes and the veteran warrior appeared much affected by the sincere welcome given him. H. II. II. the Duke l)e Nemours, was in the Ambassador's box at the Abbey, þÿ half a million of people were in the streets thro' which the jrocession passed ; þÿ and such was their good nature and orderly behaviour, that no riot or

accident occurred, and the presence of the militaiy and police were rendered unnecessary. The piocession reached the palace at 5 o'clock on its return-- a fair took place in the Park and brilliant fire works were displayed hi the evening, and superb illuminations ol the whole city closed this magnificent ceremony.

From the Montreal Courier of Saturday At noon yesterday, His Excellency the Governor General landed at the Government wharf opposite the barracks, as had been announced the day before. The crowd assembled to behold the landing was as great as Montreal could well furnish. The day being delightfully fine, the wharves for a considerable distance were crowded with spectators, as also were the streets on the way to the Government House. The regular troops in garrison, not on duty, were all under arms, and lined the streets as a guard of honor, from the wharf to the Government House. The grenadier company of the Royals, and the 7th Hussars, were drawn up on the wharf, where Major General Clitherow, with the officers of his staff, and a considerable number of civilians, awaited his excellency's landing. As his lordship's boat left the steamboat, the yards of the Medea steam frigate were manned, and a salute fired from the John Bull, the island and tiie barracks þÿ the last by the volunteer artillery. On landing, his lordship was received with the most enthusiastic cheers, þÿ which were almost constantly kept up, as he passed along the streets. Ladv Durham and family, Vice Admiral Sir Charles Paget, and the officers of his excellency's suite landed with his excellency ; and die Hussars escorted the whole party from the wharf, ihe ladies in the earl's carriage, and his lordship and the gentlemen on horseback. At 3, P M. a very numerous deputation of

the citizens of Montreal waited upon his excellency, witli the address voted on the 13th ult. whifch had been most generally signed. After reading fiis answer, His Lordship addressed himself to the deputation, in a less formal manner, stating in language to which we regret that we cannot in a memoriter report do any justice. Referring to the reception he had just met wilh in Montreal, he remarked that he had never on any occasion, through a long political life, felt more gratified by any expression of public seniiment. than lie bad been by that which lie bud just received. He assured the deputation, in the strongest terms, that the interests which they represented were interests which it was his settled determination to promote to the utmost of his power, so far as justice and a regard to the rights of others would allow ; and farther, that he was satisfied that by measures of the strictest justice they might and would be most essentially promoted. The members of the deputation were then severally introduced to his Lordship, at his own request, by Mr. Mc'Gill. The reply to the address was received by the deputation with applause ; and his Lordship's subsequent remarks were repeatedly and warmly applauded. We are ceitainly not wrong in saving, that the impression they produced on all present, was of the strongest and most favorable character. We must repeat our regret that we cannot do them justice in reporting them. About. 4' p. rn., after receiving a visit from

the Gatholic clergy of the city, who waited upon him after the deputation left, his Lordship left the Government House, and returned to the John Bull, accompanied nearly as before. We quote Lord Durham's answer to the address, as affording slicing and explicit inti- j

from the New York Commercial Advertiser, June 18, 1838. The Great Western VERY I. ATE FROM ENGLAND. The steam-ship Great Western arrived earlv yesterday morning from Bristol, having sailed from that port on the evening of the 2d inst., and consequently made the passage in fourteen days The passage from New York to Bristol was made in fourteen days, and without accident. Our papers by these arrivals are exceedingly numerous By the Great Western we have London to the evening of the 1st June, Paris to the 2!)th of May, Liverpool and Bristol to the 2d of June, all inclusive, The directors of the Great Western steam ship company have passed a resolution that another great steam vessel be immediately commenced, which is to be called 'I he City of New York. The British Queen sttam-ship was launched on the 24th of May. Col. Webb, who was a passenger in the Great Western, writes that nearly day a and a half was lost, in consequence of breaking part of the machinery of one of her engines þÿ which was, however, effectually repaired on board the ship þÿ she having a regular furnace, &c. for that purpose. The accident arose from the ignorance of her engineer, in attempting to cool one of the brasses which had become heated, bv throwing cold water upon it. He has since been discharged. It will be remembered that her chief engineer died in tiie hospital in this city before she sailed for Bristol. During the time of making the repairs the Other engine was kept at work, and so little inconvenience was experienced by the passengers from the accident, and such ample

means were at once at hand to remedy it, that a still stronger feeling of security among those on board was the consequence. We find the following correspondence in the English papers. ' Bristoi,. May 22. 1838. " To James Hosken Esq. R N. « sir þÿ The undersigned passengers on board the steam ship Great Western, on her first voyage from the U. States to England, having already expressed their conviction of the success of the great experiment of navigating the Atlantic ocean by steam, and thus facilitating the intercourse between the old and ttic new world, and securing to the inhabitants of both the advantages arising from this new era in the history of science and enterprise combined, beg leave to tender to you, sir, their greatful acknowledgments lor the satisfaction and comfort they have experienced on board your ship, and also for your kindness as a commander, and the vigilance with which you have watched over our safety. As our voyage has now reached its termination, a voyage which may more justly be denominated a pleasure excursion from New York to Bristol, we ask your acceptance of a piece of plate, as a slight testimonial of our regard 15 for vour personal character, and just . appreciation of one who has been so greatly instrumental in bringing to a successful termination this highly important experiment. " With the kindest wishes for your future prosperity. « We remain, very respectfully, yours, &c. (Signed by 53 <>f the passengers) On board the steam ship Great Western,
" Bristol Harbor, May, 1838. « To Jamks Hosken, Esq. R. N."

"We the u idersigned, passengers in the steam-ship Great Western, have the pleasure, to congratulate you on the arrival ol the noble ship under your command, in this harbor, after a short and pleasant passage trom New York. We beg leave to express to you our thanks for the exercise of those kind and gentle qualities by which you have so essentially contributed to our comfort and happiness during the voyage. We would also announce, through you to the public, that the anticipations of security and comfort, which were derived from observing the size and apparent strength of this beautiful ship, the power and proportion of her machinery, and the splendor of her accommodations, have been more than realized by a residence of fourteen days on board of her, on the bosom of the Atlantic " We would farther remark that it is in our opinion, only necessary to make a single voyage in this noble vessel, to be satisfied that complete success will attend the navigation of the Atlantic by steam, with safety, comfort and despatch. " Having performed this agreeable duty, we besr leave to offer our best wishes for your health and happiness, and have the honor to be very faithfully. " Your friends and servants." The Prince de Joinville. þÿ His honor the Mayor having been officially informed of the Prince's arrival, immediately waited on him and invited him to visit the City Hall. At

half past one o'clock, the Prince, accompanied by Commodore Casey, Captain Rosamel, Lieutenants Las Casas and Mareuil, Doctor Folleville, Mr. Pageot, Mr. Deiaforest, the French consul, and some other French gentlemen, waited on the Mayor at his office in the City Hall. The Mayor complimented the Prince upon his visit to the United States, and expressed a hope that the mutual kind feeling and good understanding which at present subsisted between France and the United States, and which was coeval with the existence of this country as an independent nation, would never experience any interruption or diminution. The Mayor then conducted the Prince to the Governor's room, where the members of the Common Council, aod several other public functionaries, had assembled to receive him After introducing him to those gentlemen, the Mayor invited the Prince and his friends to partake of a collation suitable to the season ; after during which they retired. On the same day the Prince was entertained by a large party of French gentlemen at the Astor Hotel. His Honor the Mayor and several other distinguished citizens were invited and attended the dinner. þÿ Journal of Commerce.

There is a plant inhabiting the vast prairies in North America, the ends of the leaves being armed with teeth, which have the power of closing up on being irritated by any substance, as. for instance, a fly ; indeed, these seem to be the natural food of the plant. A French philosopher engaged in the investigation of its properties put many of these plants in situations where ihev could not get any insects, and they gradually faded. He also fed some of them with beet scrapings, and these plants throve well.

animal food. A most erroneous idea has prevailed regarding the use of animal food, which has been considered as best calculated to render mankind robust and courageous. This is disproved by observation. The miserable and timid inhabitants of Northern Europe and Asia are remarkable for their moral and physical debility although they chiefly live on fish or raw flesh ; whereas the athletic Scotch and Irish are certainly not weaker than their English neighbours though consuming but little meat. The strength and agility of the negroes are well known, and the South Sea islanders, can vie in bodily exercises with our stoutest seamen ; and we have reason to believe that, at the most glorious periods of Grecian and Roman power, their armies principally subsisted upon bread, vegetables, and fruit. þÿ Millingen's Curiosities of Medical Experience.

Ttie doctor commenced by silently indicating with his nose that her fish had passed the state in which a man's olfactories could indure their flavour. '1 he Billingsgate lady made a verbal attack common in vulgar parlacc. The doctor answer" ed, ' You are an article, Madam ' No more an article than yourself, you villain.' 'You are a noun, woman' ' You þÿ you þÿ you' þÿ stammered the woman, choked with rage at a list of titles she could not understand. 'You arc a pronoun.' The beldame shook her first in a speechless rage. ' You are a verb þÿ an adverb þÿ an adjective þÿ a conjunction þÿ preposition þÿ an interjection solemnly continued the doctor, applying the harmless epithets at intervals. The nine parts of speech com. pletely conquered the old woman, and she plumpled herself into the mud, Cry-ing with rage at being thus attacked in a sot of unknown terms which, not understanding, she could not answer.

From the Albany Argus. FROM THE FRONTIER. The following is a copy of a proclama- " tion" recently issued by the leader of the gang that destroyed the steamboat Sir Robert Heel. It was obtained for Gov. Marcy ' and, if the facts may be relied on, is important, as showing that the attack, although made in the American waters, was concerted in and proceeded from the British dominions. " To all whom it may concern þÿ discovered, lurking " T William Johnson, a natural born citizen of Upper Canada, certify that 1 hold a commission in the Patriot service of Upper Canada, as commander-in-chief of the naval forces and flotilla. T commanded the expedition that captured and destroyed the steamer Sir Robert Peel. The men under my command in that expedition were nearly all natural born English subjects þÿ the exceptions were volunteers for the expedition. My Head Quarters was on an islan<l in the St. Lawrence, without the jurisdiction of the United States, at a place named by me Fort Wallace. I am well acquainted with the boundary line, and know which of the islands do, and which do not, belong to the United

States ; and in the selection of the island 1 wished to be positive, and not locate within the jurisdiction of the United States, and had reference to the decision of the commissioners under the 6th article of the treaty of Ghent, done at Utica, in the stale of New York, 13th June, 1822. 1 know the number of the Island, and by that decision it was British territory. I yet hold possession of that station, and we also occupy a station some twenty or more miles from the boundary line of the United States, in what was her Majesty's dominions until it was occupied by us. þÿ I act under orders The object of my movements is the independence of the Canadas. I am not at war with the commerce or property of the citizens of the United States " Signed this tenth day of June, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and thirty eight. « WILLIAM JOHNSON." The following is an extract from a letter from Sackett's llarbor in the Journal of Commerce of this morning. " The excitement growing out of the recent outrage on the Sir Robert Peel still continues, and occupies all minds. Refugees from Ca nada, estimated at about filteen hundred, are scattered along this frontier, and for months have been secretly but busily engaged in preparations for an incursion into Canada. It is to be regretted that they have kept alive among our citizens a good deal of the sympathy at first manifested for what was termed the patriot cause. The piratical conduct of these last desperadoes has had a good ellect

in rectifying, to same extent, an erroneous state of public feeling, but it has not as yet been entirely efficacious. The greater part of the offenders have been arrested, but the ringleaders are not yet taken, and they probably owe their success in eluding justice, in some measure, to the interfering sympathy of our people. Most of those who are still at large have taken refuge among the " Thousand Islands" in the river St. Lawrence, and 1 can assure you it will be a very difficult and dangerous matter to dislodge them. What are called the " Thousand Islands," are in truth about seventeen hundred, extending some thirty miles up and down the St. Lawrence; and bv their peculiar formation and location, they present the most secure retreat for freebooters that can be found in any quarter of the globe " " These desperate men cannot be driven off without a military and naval force of considerable power. The islands have high rocky shores, are covered with a dense wood( separated by narrow, winding and intricate channels, and full of of fastnesses of great na. tural stri ngth. The present possessors have numerous places, very difficult to be are provided with water craft well adapted to their service, well armed and plentifully provided with ammunition and provisions. Their leader, William Johnson, seems to be, from all accounts, admirably designed by character, and fitted by education and habit, for the enterprise in which he is engaged Hardy, bold and resolute, he recklessly pursues the objects he has in

view. He professes to be well aware of the perils he encounters, acknowledges the desperateness of his cause, and avows his belief that he shall lose his life in its prosecution þÿ He declares that he will not be taken alive, and has notified those who are on the search for him, that they must bring their coffins with thctn."

He is literally armed " cap a pie" þÿ carries six pistols about his person, repeating rifle, a dirk and bowie knife. His row-boat is nearly forty feet in length, made of white cedar, has eight oars, and exceeds in speed, on trial, the fastest steamboat on the lake. ' He declares that he is at war with the Queen of Great Britain, for the redress of injuries received from her Canadian subjects ; that his warfare is honorable, and that he acts under a commission received from the patriot government. He bids fair to be as renowned in buccaneering history as Captain Kidd. I am interrupted, and must abruptly close my description of the hero of the Thousand Islands.

Canadian Troubles. þÿ It is barely possible that we may yet be involved in a war with England, growing out of the recent disturbances in Canada and along the þÿfrontier we say this is only possible, because there is too much good sense in the great mass of the People of both nations, and too much good feeling between the two Governments, to allow of its probability. Still, the incendiaries and conspirators on both sides of the lines, who have done all in their power to instigate a war, deserve hanging just as thoroughly as if they had been successful. Their intent is clearly malignant and blood-thirsty ; and if any way could be found to bring them within the power of the law, the example and the effect could not fail of being most salutary. The town of Lewiston and its journal have been conspicuous in their efforts to fan the embers of Canadian insurrection ; and we understand they are now reaping the fruits of their conduct in the loss of the large amount of frontier travel, as well directly across as from Albany to Niagara by way of Lake Ontario. The last paper protests that there is no danger of delay or molestation in that quarter. The Robert Peel and Brockvillc outrages would seem to tell a different story. There are other journals on our own frontier which have held throughout a language totally unjustifiable in relation to the hostile expeditions set on foot from our territory, and the refugees which were for months at work to set on foot those expeditions. We are

surprised and mortified at the general tone of the press of Northern Vermont on this subject. The most intemperate and abusive denunciations of the British Canadian Government have been indulged in, and the designs of the agitators countenanced to an extent wholly at variance with national amity and good feeling, and destructive of the intimate and friendly commercial and political relations heretofore subsisting. We say nothing of the sympathy felt for the Patriots and the anxiety evinced for their success ; that is matter of opinion, and every man will think as he pleases ; but aiding the fugitive insurgents to disturb and alarm the Canadian frontier and to fit out hostile armaments within the territory of the United States, is so clearly a violation of treaties and of the law of nations that we see not how it can be countenanced by any pcaceloving and conscientious citizen. In this connexion, we may as well notice the dirty outrage said to have been recently Committed at Detroit. A party of British military officers were over on a visit, when they were assailed in the streets by parcel a of inconceivably shameless blackguards, and pelted with mud, filth, and rotten eggs, until they sought shelter on board a ferry-boat. þÿ The beings who could stoop to this dastardly, brutal meanness, would not hesitate to set their own city on fire and swear it on the British, in order to provoke a war Does not every man sec that such conduct tends directly to a fcaiful calamity þÿ a calamity

which cannot be incurred without piling mountains of guilt and blood on the souls of those who invoke it ? þÿ We have thus far spoken of the errors on our own side of the boundary ; those on the other are equally numerous if not equally glaring. It is manifest that iho British do not inow how to govern a province like Canada

OOBia'-RliTBS AT13 --but that is their business. We remark on it only as it endangers the preservation of peace. But misgovernnient in any country where a spirit of resistance has been awakened is always perilous to its immediate neighbors, and therefore a legitimate subject of comment. We understand that Great Britain has spent from twenty-five to thirty millions of dollars within the last six months in what she calls maintaining her authority in Canada, and protecting her subjects from insurrection and invasion. Three-fourths of this has been as clearly thrown away as the twenty millions that we have so beautifully buried in the morasses of Florida. In the first place, there need have been no rebellion if her Governors had understood their business, and been as intent on discharging their duty as maintaining their dignity ; in the next, there has been no occasion for this lavish expenditure. But for the audacious burning of the Caroline in an American port þÿ an act of consummate insolence and folly three-fourths of this treasure might þÿ have been saved. Her Maiden Majesty may make the leader in that exploit a Duke if she will ; the act will still be an indefensible one. To talk of that steamboat and her crew as pirates is the extreme of folly. We are the proper judges of the character of an American vessel lying at anchor in an American port ; and when British authorities assume to cut such a one out at the dead of night, drive ofl the crew with deadly weapons, and burn her, they are quite too careful of our morals.

Besides, their own conduct refutes this shallow subterfuge If the Caroline were a pirate, why was not her crew detained for trial? Why were even those carried away prisoners released the next day ? The pretext falls to the ground. But a new Governor General has been sent over, with Dictatorial powers; and we have been favored with a few touches of his quality. We regret say to that they are not very promising. From the little we know of his previous character. Lord Durham would seem about the worst man that the British Ministry could have selected for this momentous trust- To begin with, a radical aristocrat is the wrong man to command in America. We speak not of mere aristocracy of position þÿ Durham is neither better nor worse for being a Lord ; while lofty birth and an illustrious ancestry are rather in his lavor. But a Noble who rises to power as a Liberal, and who is yet fanatical in his requirement of homage from inferiors, and in the enforcement of all those petty acknowledgments of deference to the great which are a practical indignity to the humble, can hardly become popular on this side of the Atlantic þÿ not even in Canada. þÿ Haughtiness of bearing and a tenacity of forms are so nearly allied to narrowness of mind, that a people accustomed to a reasonable share of social equality if not of political freedom will be very apt to confound them, and to infer the latter from, the former.

We regret to perceive already the evidences of Lord þÿDurham s unfitness for his new position. He began by dissolving the old Executive Council þÿ which was right þÿ and organizing a new one of his immediate satellites and þÿretainers which was wrong. He is thus at this moment vested with a power over British America as despotic as that of Nicholas over Russia. His Inaugural Proclamation is a windy document, which abounds in grandiloquent sentences, yetdeve-

lopes nothing of his proposed policy except that he will do just what pleases him. That we understood before. But so far he keeps on his own ground. His later Proclamation, however þÿ the one offering a reward of one thousand pounds for the apprehension of the destroyers of the Sir Robert Peel þÿ taken in connexion with the Siamese display of his man Sir George Arthur, (which appeared in our last) þÿ is of a far more exceptionable character. The two indicate a mutual ignorance of the condition of affairs on the frontier, if not of the laws of nations, which are deplorable in the occupants of such important stations.

The Crops. þÿ The general prospect is still highly favorable, though in some districts injury from insects and from rats is apprehended. The Alexandria Gazette of Tuesday says þÿ þÿ -Nothing can exceed the beauty and promise of the growing crops in the adjacent counties of Virginia. We have just had an opportunity of seeing some of the finest wheat fields in Loudoun that we ever saw, and we hear that all around the same prospect is presented. There has been rain enough, and a few warm days will make and secure the wheat."

Lord Durham, it is reported, has sent home to England for 12,000 more troops! His Lordship does not seem to understand that to govern men on this Continent requires brains rather than muskets. Mi. John Van Huron, son of the President, has gone over to attend Queen þÿVictoria s corronation, and some papers are making very silly remarks upon it. Who has a better right.
Queen Victoria has paid her father's debt, and presented the creditors with a beautiful piece of plate.
Lord Ward, a young English nobleman who has just come of age, is said to possess an income of more than two hundred thousand pounds sterling per annum, or about two dollars per minute.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, July 2ih Marshal Soult's Tuir to tiie Manufacturing Districts. þÿ His Excellency and suite left Birmingham on Tuesday morning, at live o'clock. In his private travelling carriage were his Excellency, Admiral and Colonel Napier, and Mr Manby ; and in the omnibus were the Marquises Dalmatia and De Mornay, Duke De Vicenza, and the rest of his suite. The party proceeded to Ivenilworth and Warwick, where they were wait-

the Town Council, and other respectable in. habitants, who were presented to the Marshal- The illustrious stranger then visited Beecham Chapel, and Kenilworth and Warwick Castles, and all the objects of interest in the neighbourhood. The Marshal was exceedingly pleased, and much struck with the fine old baronial residence here, it being the first of the kind he had seen since his arrival in England. The beauty of the surrounding scenery was also much admired by his Excellency and suite. After breakfasting, the party again set out on their rapid tour, and at the main road Daventry, they found relays of their own post-horses ready. At Stoney Stratford the party were met by Mr. Bagster and Mr H nine, to whose excellent arrangements along the line much credit was given- At this place one of the wheels of the Marshal's carriage broke, which, considering the tremendous pace at which the party went, w is by no means surprising. A short delay till matters were set right, was the only inconvenience sustained bv the accident, and the carriages reached the railway, in gallant style, about four o'clock, and thence to London at half-past five in the afternoon. When the route of the distinguished strangers was first marked out in London, Mr. Manby undertook to have the whole ground gone over, every object of interest examined, and the party back to London at four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon þÿ a task which he would have literally accomplished to the minute, had it not been for the accident at Stoney

Stratford We believe the excursion is unin this or any other country, and the astonishment of the distinguished strangers was frequently expressed to those about them. þÿ Along the line at Warwick, Daventry, Stoney Stratford, Denbigh Hall, and the various rail- Way stations, the crowds collected were im" niense. In St >ncy Stratford more especially, it was with some difficulty that the carriages could be driven through the streets. Cheerings and acclamations marked the progress of the illustrious stranger during their entire route, exhibiting more strongly the honourable and generous character of the English people, and their anxiety to bury all former differences, and extend the right hand of fellowship to the gallant warrior who had come among them as a friend and a citizen, than the most laboured and well turned periods could express. At every town and district visited by the Marshal in his route, all parties who had the honour of being presented, wore unanimous in their praise of the marked condescension and kindness with which they received by the Marshal, the Marquis Dalmatia, Marquis De Mornay, and the other members of the party. The elegance and politeness of the ve.ille cour, were combined with so much of the warmth and cordiality of the English nation, in his greetings, that it was said by one gentleman at Liverpool--" the Marshal

JBACTSr TUB3!P23T3D3Sa: WMWaWLMtoS had achieved a greater triumph over the prejudices of the English people by his personal intercourse with them than he could have effected at the head of 100,000 men." The Marshal expressed himself deeply indebted for the attention he had received from the directors of the London and Birmingham Kailway Company, who had acted with a liberality which might be in vain looked for from any other private company in the world.

IMPORTANT FROM HAVANA. From the New Orleans Commercial Bulletin. Troubles in Havana. þÿ The steam ship Natchez having been detained at Key West paralleled for speed in the annals of travelling for want of fuel, a schooner was despatched to Havana to procure a supply of coal. The officer sent in command of the schooner stated, on his return to Key West, that there had been some serious disturbances among i mont would not be hazardous, if not the troops at Havana. The circumstances and particulars had been kept a secret, as far as possible, by the public authorities, so that nothing certain Lad transpired as to the cause or origin ol the affair. This much is ascertained, that a conspiracy was detected among the troops and officers of several regiments garrisoning the Moro Gastle, through the treachery of one of the individuals implicated. They were, it was supposed, dissatisfied with the removal of Gen. Tacon ; but this is all conjecture. The discovery of the treason led to the most vigorous measures, on the part of the new Governor, Esihiliita, to crush it in the bud. The gates were immediately shut upon the regiments in their barracks, and the fort which they garrisoned converted into their prison. Eighty of the ringleaders were seized and executed on the, spot, and as many more detained under arrest, awaiting a confirmation of their guilt. From the frequent and heavy firing heard from the Fort, it was supposed that a severe conflict took place between the conspirators and the Government force. In Havana, the
disturbance produced among the inhabitants

great agitation and excitement, heightened by the mystery with which it was shrouded. On the departure of the schooner, all was quiet ; the insurrection having been eth dually put down by the energy and promptitude of Gov. Espeleta.

FURTHER FROM HAVANA. From the New Orleans Commercial Bulletin , August 10. The Conspiracy at Havana. þÿ A letter received by a commercial house in this city from a correspondent at Havana, confirms the statement published in the Bulletin of yesterday. The writer says that a Garlist conspiracy had been detected among some of the regiments stationed at Havana, and many arrests and executions had taken place. From this it would seem that we were mistaken as to the cause of the revolt, as originating in dissatisfaction with the removal of Gen. Tacon. The object of the conspirators was to wrest the Government of Cuba from the (ueen, arid place it in the hands of Don Carlos.

Mr. J Wise went up Saturday afternoon, at Philadelphia, in his Parachute Balloon, and, according to his account, after reaching 13,000 feet, finding himself in a thunder storm, the balloon exploded from its great expansion and lie descended by means of the parachute apparatus in safety, near Easton. We subjoin Mr. Wise's account of his perilous excursion. It is full of interest : þÿ

PERILOUS BALLOON DESCENT. Office of the Argus, Easton, Aver. 13. On Saturday last, 1 Ith inst at 10 minutes before 12 o'clock, I ascended, with my Parachute Balloon, accompanied with two small Parachutes and animals, from the spacious yard ot the Washington Hotel, kept bv Mr. (.on nor, and as soon as I attained the height ol 2000 feet, 1 detached the conical parachute with its occupant, which landed in safety near the La Fayette College ; by that time I rose several thousand feet more, when 1 detached my oiled silk parachute which experiment was to decide the certain! v and safety of my parachute balloon. It did j not descend with that uniform velocity as the J first. 1 however concluded that the experidisagreeable. I also was satisfied by former deseonts, that a balloon as soon as it became flaccid would invert, in a rapid descent When I attained an altitude of about 13,000 feet, the balloon became fearfully expanded, causing a loud hissing from the small tube at the bottom, through which the valve rope passed, giving me warning that unless 1 opened my safey valve, the balloon must rupture; at this critical moment I became somewhat excited as 1 looked over the side of mv car and saw the vivid flashes of lightning passing from one cloud to another. The thunder gust was moving from S. W. to N. W. and mv vessel, at this time, was sailing swiltlv from N' W. towards. E. passing New Village and Asbury I looked at my time-piece, and found it 2(1 minutes past 2, and as I was re-

turning it to my pocket, the balloon exploded! Although 1 had confidence in the apparatus, 1 must admit that it was a moment ol awful suspense, for in the space of 10 seconds the gas rushed from the balloon with the noise resembling the approach of a hurricane, and as I fell through the air it whistled through the nut work like unto a strung north wester,

throuirh the rigging of a ship. I cast my eves to the balloon, and found my expectations realized, ft assumed the form of a concave hemisphere, falling rapidly without any vibratory motion, until 1 reached the lower strata of air, which was blowing a sharp gale from the South. When the parachute commenced its first vibrations, drilling me northward, making a vibration about every ten seconds, which now made the descent very unpleasant, every motion causing a sensation similar to that of a person dreaming he is falling. The wind from the south drifted me about ihroe miles before I approached the earth, and made my landing much harder than it would have been in a calm atmosphere. As 1 neared the earth, I threw over all my ballast, which put me off my guard, and as mv car struck the earth obliquely, it bounced me out about ten feet slightly bruising my shoulder. I sprang on my feet quickly to see it collapse, but it had fell alongside of me. I now stood gazing with astonishment, first at the parachute, then at the car, which had turned bottom upwards. 1 next east my eyes to the fleeting clouds through which 1 was sailing but three minutes before, and now t was standing on terra firma, congratulating myself on the result of my experiment, which i intend soon to repeat I landed on the farm of Mr. Elijah Warne, about 10 mites from Easton, and got the assistance of Mr. Warne and his neighbors, who were watching the descent of the parachute, little thinking that a human being accompanied it.
J. WISE.

The Great Western is again on the ocean. She sailed from New York on Thursday al. ternoon, during a heavy rain storm. Her departure is thus noticed by the Evening Star. James A. Dickson, Esq. of this city is among her passengers : þÿ The Great Western steamship took her departure at half past 4 yesterday afternoon in fine þÿstyle in spite of the stiff blow from South by East, much rain and dirty looking weather, all of which detained the packets in port. She came round from the East River with her British, American and French colors at mast head, and moved with great elegance, her quarter deck covered with passengers, and her hull scarcely having the appearance of being sunk at all in the water. On the Battery there were thousands collected to see her cleaving so swiftly through a head wind directly in her teeth, and (for our bay) a heavy sea that was constantly splashing up its breakers on the Battery Terrace. As she went up the river past the Battery she fire a gun, then rounded the two French vessels, the Didon hoisting the British ensign, when the Great Western fired again and was answered by the frigate þÿ She now proceded onward with great beauty down the hay on her course to the sea, followed by the Passaic and one or two other steamers crowded with passengers. The Great Western as she passed the Didon gave an opportunity of comparing her length, which is some 10 to 15 ieet longer than that large sized frigate. Every one was struck with the steady movement

and handsome appearance of the steam ship, as she was seen to great advantage, by every object looming up stronger and brighter from the humid state of the atmosphere. She carried 80 passengers, and her letter postage amounts to $2000.

From the London Times, Wednesday , Amgast 15, 1S38. Private letters from Warsaw, dated the 20th ult. have arrived. They contain a reference to an extraordinary conspiracy said to have been detected in the Polish capital (denounced by the French Government, as it was believed), and to which was attributed the numerous arrests that had lately taken place in Warsaw and elsewhere in Poland ( see The Times of the 2d instant). From these letters it would appear that the intention of the conspirators þÿ among whom, as we have already mentioned, were several Russian officers þÿ was to blow up the Emperor in the fortress of Rola, which it was known he would visit, or rather to visit which was the chief object of his journey. As. however, our correspondent cannot vouch for the facts to which he refers, we omit tor the present the publication of his letter.

Our Paris correspondence mentions that JV1. Fabricius leit that city at 4 o'clock on Sunday afternoon, for the Hague in the first instance, whence he would proceed to Nassau, of which state he had been in Paris the Charge d'Atfaires. Our correspondent mentions that the circumstances attending the departure of M. Fabricius were of an allecting kind. He and his family had resided in Paris during 37 years, and had formed there extensive connexions. There would appear to be, on the part of the French Government, an intention to suggest to the public a belief that 'he affair of Belgium and Holland might possiblv lead to hostilities. On day small detachments of artillery, from various regiments qunrteied in districts remote from e h other, are stated to have receive orders to proceed to the northern frontier. One another, a General (Delort) who was about to proceed to visit the department of the Seine on local business is mentioned as having been commanded to make a tour of inspection on the "eastern" frontier Our Paris letters repeat, however, that " no apprehension on the subject was really entertained, although more time would be spent in bringing the Hollando-Belgic question to its termination than had probably been contemplated." The Emperor ol Russia, bv an ukase dated Fischbache, in Silesia, July 1 1, had decreed a levy of six men out of every thousand in the northern provinces of the empire, for the service of the army and navy. The lew is to be completed on the 13th of January, lb39.

I'AGANINI'S FOURTH STRING. In order to refute the many tales and rumors relative to the occasion which induced the celebrated virtuoso to acquire such a wonderful power of execution on the fourth string of the violin, an Italian publication has lately given the following particulars, professedly in the words of the great master himself ; þÿ " At Lucca I always led the orchestra whenever the reigning family attended the opera. 1 was also frequently sent into the Court circle, and I gave a grand concert every fortnight The Princess Eliza (Bar.ciocclii, Napoleon's sister) always retired before the conclusion, because the harmonic notes of my instrument alTected her nerves too powerfully. A verv amiable lady, whom 1 had long since secretly adored, was frequently present at these parties, and 1 soon perceived that a pleasing secret attracted her also to me. Our mutual passion imperceptibly gained strength. One day I promised in the next concert to surprise her with a musical piece of gallantry, which should have a reference to the terms upon which we stood At the same time I caused the Gourt to he apprized that I meat to perform a new composition, with the title of ' A Love Scene ' General curiosity was excited ; but what was the amazement of the company when I entered with a violin which had but two strings! I had left only the G and the E string. The latter was intended to express all the feelings of a young female ; the former to imitate the voice of a despairing lover. In this manner I executed

a kind of impassioned dialogue, in which the tenderest tones succeeded expressions of jealousy. At one time they were caressing þÿ at another, tearful accords, cries of anger and of rapture, of pain and of felicity. A reconciliation formed th close ; the lovers, more enamoured than ever of each other, performed a pas de dear, which terminated in a brilliant coda. This 'Scene' was highly applauded. I say nothing of the delighted looks which the lady of my thoughts cast upon me. The Princess Eliza, after loading me w ith praises, said to me, flatteringly. " You have done the impossible on two strings ; would not a single one be enough for your talent I" I promised immediately to make the trial This idea flattered my imagination, and in a few weeks 1 composed for the fourth string a sonata entitled Napoleon, which 1 performed on the 25th of August, before a numerous and brilliant court. The success surpassed my expectations. From that tine dates my predilection for the G string. People were never tired of listening to my pieces composed for that at) ing. As one keeps learning from day to day, so I gradually alt lined that proficiency, in which there ought now to be nothing astonishing.'1

Changf. of Haik. þÿ There are several instances of the hair having suddenly been changed from its natural color from a strong attention of the mind. The Duke ofSullo, in his in in urs. relates that Henry IV. told the Marquis de la Force, that when he heard the edict commanding all llugenots to attend mass on pain of banishment, the mustachoe turned white on that side of his face which he was leaning on his hand. A more genera! effect happened to a man in one of the western islands, who was descending a rock to gather sea fowls' nests. While he was suspended in the air by a rope, he was attacked by two eagles who had their eyrie in the crag, and making a stroke at them with his dirk, severed the rope over his head to a single ply ; he immediately made the signal to be drawn up, and was recovered in safety; but when he reached the summit of the rock, his hair had turned grey with fear. It was told of Mr. Palmer, once postmaster in Ireland ; that having suffered some reflections upon the Duke of Portland, and having vainly demanded satisfaction from that nobleman, in the night he refused to fight, his hair was entirely turned grey. A similar change happened to the Count de I. as Cases on the night after he learnt of the banishment of the Emperor Napoleon to St. Helena. It is told of a German nobleman, that on the night of his condemnation to death, his hair turned as white as flax. A less rated and more ignoble instance was Maccoul, the robber of Paisley Bank, and supposed murderer of Bigby,
whose hair in the last three months of his life, changed trom jet black to silver grey.

BAsrm From the St. Thomas Times, Wednesday September 29 1838. THE FORGED STATE PAPERS.

(From the Paris Correspondent of the Times.) The Courier Francais contains no article on the affair of Fabricius and Chaltas. You would not credit the extent to which Chaltas carried his manufactory, nor the variety of points to which his forged articles were directed, nor the amount of documents supplied bv him. They range from 1832 to the present time the 18th July, 1838, is the date of the last. They refer to almost every political topic subject. or The Spanish war þÿ the Belgian question (at two epochs) þÿ the occupation of Ancona and finally, the coro- þÿ nation of her Majesty Queen Victoria. On the Spanish question the articles he supplied were contradictions of the telegraphic dispatches (particularly that which announced the death of Zumalacarregui), correspondence from the head-quartei s of Don Carlos (a portion of which purported to be written by that prince himself), &c. M. Chaltas had been for some years a prisoner in the debtors prison (in St. Pelagie and the Rue de Clichv) for damages, costs, and fines incurred by a libel on the Duke of Brunswick. His discharge occurred about six weeks since. The police had previously been on the scent, and fairly ran him down, as you know, on yesterday se'nnight. It does not appear when exactly his acquaintance with M. Fabricius commenced, nor is it clear that it was to that diplomats that all the ducuments known to have been forged were furnished, but copies of upwards of 200 are at this moment before the J age dTnstructiori, who is charged with prosecut-

ing the affair. The proceedings so commenced will not, however, be persevered in. There are too many interests compromised too many private matters narrated to render a public prosecution politic or discreet. Before I refer to the part of the business that will most interest you, 1 shall inform you that M. Fabricius was made to believe that the papers furnished him were abstracted from the Foreign office by a principal clerk ( chef de division), " whose mistress took advantage of his sleep or absence to copy them." During the period of Chaltas' imprisonment a woman in that character handed them herself to M. Fabricius. Afterwards Chaltas conveyed them to him. Immediately on the arrest of Chaltasi Count Mole (President of the Council and Minister for Foreign Affairs), sent for M. Fabricius, and, as you already know, showed him the whole of the proofs of his connexion with the affair. Amongst other documents placed by Count Mol ' in M. Fabricius' hands, were two letters of M. Fabricius himself to Challas, in which he complained that "the quality of the article was disapproved of by his (M Fabricius') constituents ( commitants ), that it came from a bad factory, and recommending him to apply to a better, and not to be deterred by any idea of expense." (It were superfluous to say that Chaltas had the power of rendering, and that he did render, the articles all that could be desired, so as to suit the taste of Fabricius' constituents) M. Fabricius was obliged to admit the truth of
the charge, and retired. In an interview with Count Mole on the day following, however, he recanted his declaration. It was

matnarj&isros then that Count Mole became so a i Munis, lit that he threatened to have him arrested as a swindler ( escrod ). Feeling that it would be necessary to prove to the Dutch government that the charges he (Count Mole) made against its minister was correct, he obtained from Chaltas, and forwarded to the Hague, a detailed statement of the whole affair, in which he stated that M. Fabricius was the person to whom the forged documents were delivered, and by whom they were paid for þÿ " the best of them at lOOOf. each." The chief document, or that which purported to be the principal one, was an alleged dispatch from General Sebastiani to Count Mole, bearing date since the coronation of her Majesty Queen Victoria. General Sebastiani is made to say in that letter that he had that morning seen Lord Palmerston ; that the British government wished to have the Belgic question settled at any price, in order to be free to direct all its attention and exertions to " the east that the British Ministry did not feel themselves much strengthened by the coronation ; that the conduct of the Tories latterly, and particularly the moderation evinced by the Duke of Wellington, had been very agreeable and acceptable to them, and that, neilher on the question of the Belgic limits, nor on that of the indemnity, would England co-operate with France, should the latter power support King Leopold in his refusal to acquiesce in the provisions of the 24 articles. To this dispatch Count Mole was made (in another letter) to reply, lamenting the infor-

mation contained in General Sebastiani's dispatch abandoning the question of limits; þÿ but desiring that General Sebastiani should make another effort to induce the British go" vcrnment to concur with France in obtaining a reduction of the amount of the indemnity awarded to Holland. þÿ General Sebastiani's rejoinder states, that he had again seen Lord Palmerston ; that he had failed to induce any alteration in the already expressed determination of the British government, and that King Leopold must accept the 24 articles purely and simply. Dispatches of M. Bresson, (the French Ambassador at Berlin) were also furnished by Chaltas to M. Fabricius. as well as the answers to those of Count Mole. M Bresson was by the latter instructed to go to Frankfort, where he would have a secret interview with the Bavarian minister on the Luxemburg question. M. Bresson writes from Frankfort that he had not seen that diplomatist, at which he is wroth ; but that he had had interviews with the most influential of the Germanic Diet, who told him that no accommodations with regard to the limits was possible, and that they understood that Austria, Prussia and Russia, would insist on the payment to Holland of the entire of the awarded indemnity. M. Bresson is made to take offence at a passage in a letter from Count Mole, and to tender his resignation, but he is appeased by an autograph letter of King Louis Philippe praying him to retain his office at a juncture so critical. Another letter of General Sebastiani prays

for leave of absence, to enable him to go to Vichy to take the waters, which are absolutely necesscry for his health. He says that he had left the matter in proper train, in the hands of M. Bourquenay, who in his absence would take care that the interests of Belgium should not suffer. To this Count Mole, in

ATas very dignified terms, replies. Count Mol6 tells the general that the King would see with the greatest pain his absence from his post at so momentous a crisis. That he (the general) had already rendered great services in the affair, and that his talents were indispensable for bringing it to a favourable issue, and entreating him to remain in London, &c. The Count, in reply, submits to the royal will, hoping that after the close of the conference he should be allowed to go to Vichy, <fco. The last of the documents 1 shall refer to is one from Marshal Soult to the King, in which he gives to his Majesty an account of an audience with which he was honoured by her Majesty Queen Victoria. In the course of that audience, the object of which was to recommend to the royal notice of the Queen the Duke de iNemours, he was happy to col. lect from the avowal of her Majesty that the prince had made a favourable impression. þÿ The marshal suggests, however, ' in order to throw dust in the eyes of the English people,' and to mask the progress the prince had made in the affection of her Majesty, that the Duke be ordered to the camp of Luneville» with the understanding that he return to London to prosecute bis suit immediately after that the camp shall break up. The marshal's letter encloses one from the Duchess of Kent addressed to the Kinsr, expressive of her roy al highness's approbation of the Duke de Nel mours for a son-in-law, her sense of the honour it would be to herself that such an

union were formed, sanctioning the marriage, and anticipating from it strength and happiness for both countries, 1 have now some serious facts to state, namely, that the communication of those forged matters to the foreign powers, for they were evidently furnished to Russia, Prussia, and Austria, so completely impeded the negociations of the Conference in London (pro. duisit une telle perturbation), that Count Sebastiani, really instructed by his court that on certain points he might expect opposition and in others acquiescence, experienced directly contrary effects When the discovery respecting Chaltas and M. Fabricius was made, Count Mole saw at once how the matter stood, and sent directions to General Sebastiani to suspend all intercourse with the other members of the Conference until all the evil impressions produced by the forgeries should have been removed. 1 have only time to add that those letters are all so well written, so much and so completely in the diplomatic style, that some unfrocked diplomatist must have aided in their construction »»>aw From the London Morning Post, Aug. 15.

England is beginning to be uneasy about her East India possessions. Russia has captured the important city of Teheran, in Persia, and it may not be long before the Russian Army may be permitted to march to the confines of that Empire. England, in reference to these gigantic strides of the Autocrat, has induced Mehemet Ali to settle his difference with Turkey. A rail road will be made from Cairo to the Red Sea, which will be navigated by steam boats to Babelmandel arid across the Indian Ocean, so that with steamers from England to Egypt, the British can throw in troops into India in fifty days.

The appearance of Victoria, or Vic., as she is familiary termed in England, is not remarkably prepossessing, though she is by no means ugly. She is quite small in stature, light complexion, blue eyes, wears her hair a la Greeque, and dresses with great simplicity. Her form is spare, and face rather distinguished for a want of animation than otherwise. Owing to a slight defect, her upper lip, is contracted, so as to expose her teeth, even when not smiling or talking : þÿ this defect, however, is but little noticed, as it lias been adopted, of course in compliment to Victoria, by all the ladies at Court, and indeed by English females generally.

Sweet soother of the cares of life, That maketh all things end in smoke, I bless thee as I would a wife When donning first the nuptial yoke: The fairest rose hath no perfume As sweet as that inhaled from thee, And Araby, in all its bloom, Could never have such charms for me.

I sit beneath a shady tree, My feet at angle forty-five, And as I draw thy sweets irom thee, 1 am the happiest man alive ; Soft floating on the sunny air, A thousand songs of birds are mine : Away, away with every care, My principle I'm wholly thine

The falsehood of the world shall not Disturb me in this hour of peace ; My soul a joy from thee hath caught, Will last until thy puffs shall cease, The smile of woman may be false, And friendship last but for a day, But thee each test alone exalts, þÿ Thou never, never canst betray.

As round my nose thy curls ascend, I build my castles in the air, So bright, 'tis pity that they end, And last but while thy smoke is there : Awhile 1 rule the world a king, Or mingle in the heady fight, While birds in lofty numbers sing The grateful praises of my might.

Or lulled in a delicious dream, To beauty's power 1 bend the knee, And loving and beloved, I dream The world is filled with joy for me ; And with my spirit's idol stray, Forgetful of the fleeting hours, Where smile, like angels on our way, The faces of a thousand flowers.

Oh love thou art the sweatest ill That ever racked the soul of man. þÿ Though sometimes thou art said to kill, Yet I will catch thee if I can. I know the prettiest þÿ zounds, my dreams Of joy have suffered an eclipse, My principe is done, it set ms I've smoked it till it burnt my lips.

Anecdote. A BLIND man having buried five hundred pounds in a corner of his garden, was robbed of them by a neighbour who saw him at work. þÿ Suspecting who had stolen his treasure he went to him, and asked his advice in the most friendly way, concerning a bag with a thousand dinars, which he said he had by him, and would gladly know his opinion about the disposal of them. " I have at present," said he, " five hundred dinars in a certain part of my garden, & I believe I shall decide upon putting thisthere likewise." His neighbour hearing this, took the first opportunity of replacing the five hundred dinars, in hopes of being able soon to draw out double the sum ; but the blind man having attained his end, put it out of his power to make a second attempt.

The American Ship Washington, h. T. Thukher, master, arrived here on Sunday last in distress, after a passage of 11 1 davs from Calcutta, bound to Philadelphia. The Ship has been leaking badly for more than 90 days, and the Olficers and crew were completely exhausted on their arrival here, by their exertions to keep her afloat. Through the politeness of a mercantile gentleman in this place, we have been favored with the loan of the Sheffield Mercury dated Aug. 18, by which we are enabled to lav before our readers the speech of Her Most Gracious Majesty Queen Victoria, on the proroguing of Parliament.

HER MAJESTY'S SPEECH. "My Lords and Gentlemen, " The state ot Public Business enables me to close this protracted and laborious Session. " I have to lament that the civil war in Spain forms an exception to the general tranquillity. I continue to receive from all Foreign Powers the strongest assurances of their desire to maintain with me the most amicable relations " The disturf 'ances and insurrections which had, unfortunately, broken out in Upper and Lower Canada, have been promptly suppressed. and 1 entertain a confident hope that firm and judicious measures will empower you to restore a Constitutional form of Government, which unhappy events have compelled you for a time to suspend. " I rejoice at the progress which has been made in mv Colonial possessions towards the entire Abolition of Negro Apprenticeship. " 1 have observed with much satisfaction the attention which you h ave bestowed upon the amendment of the Domestic Institutions of the Country. 1 trust that the mitigation of the law of Imprisonment for Debt will prove at once favourable to the liberty of my subjfects, and safe for commercial credit ; and that the Established Church will derive increased strength and efficacy from the restriction of the granting of Benefices in Plurality. " 1 have felt great pleasure in giving my assent to the Bill for the relief of the destitute poor in Ireland. I cherish the expectation that its provisions have been so cautiously framed, and will be so prudently executed,

that whilst they contribute to relieve distress, they will tend to preserve order, and to encourage habits of industry and exertion. " I trust likewise that the Act which you have passed relating to the Composition for Tithes in Ireland, will increase the security of that property, and promote internal peace. " Gentlemen of the House Commons, of " I cannot sufficiently thank you for your dispatch and liberality providing foi the in expense my household and the maintenance of of the honor and dignity of the Crown. I offer you my warmest acknowledgments for the addition which you have made to the income of mv beloved Mother. " I thank you for the Supplies which you have voted for the ordinary Public Service, as well as for the readiness with which you

2>AJT3X TESTISTMSIR have provided means to meet, the extraordinary expenses rendered necessary by the state of my Canadian possessions. " My Lords and Gentlemen, " The many useful measures which you have been able to consider, while the settlement of the Civil List, and the state of Canada demanded so much of your attention, are a satisfactory proof of your zeal for the public good. You are so well acquainted with the duties w hich now devolve upon you in your respective counties, that it is unnecessary to remind you of them. In the discharge of them you may scarcely rely upon my firm support, and it only remains to express an humble hope that Divine Providence may watch over us ail, and prosper our united efforts for the welfare of our country. The Lord Chancellor announced that the Parliament stood prorogued till Thursday, the llih day of October.

( From the London Times, August 15.) Petition of Canadian Prisoners to Lord Durham. þÿ The following are the extracts trom Mr. C. Buller's letter alluded to by Mr. Leader in the House ot Commons : þÿ " I enclose you our fiist great act about the prisoners. It will appear to you horribly unconstitutional and despotic, but it is really mild. We put no one to death. Our transportation is, you will see, not to be penal, but merely accompanied by measures necessary for security. The rest are merely banished ; we confiscate no property. We were obliged to include a great many in our provision, in conformity to a general rule laid down in each case, whom we do not wish and do not intend to treat so hardly. This is rather an advantage, as it will enable ns immediately to bring the pardoning power into operation. We would not interfere with the ordinary tribunals or tamper with the juries. The legal guilt of these men w as clear From an ordinary jury their certain acquittal was equally clear. These ignorant Canadians would have said either that their leaders in the revolt were right all along, or that the Government had not dared to punish The British party would have said that our trial had been a more mockery ofjust'ce, and that j we had let their guilty enemies loose on them j by a trick. Our present act does something like substantial justice: it will do good to both parties, and in no way corrupt the great | ralls aims I UoodchihCs children. Judicial institutions of the country.
