SCENES IN THE LIFE or NAPOLEON. battle of leip9ic. " ' This day,' said the Emperor as he mounted his horse, this day will resolve a great question. The destiny of France is about to be decided on the field of Leipsie. þÿ Should we be victorious, all our misfortunes may yet be repaired ; should we be conquered, it is impossible to foresee what may be the consequences of our defeat.' All the officers of the escort might have heard these words " About noon we were attacked on all points by the whole combined forces of the allies. Our army, reduced to less than a hundred thousand men, had to oppose a force of three hundred and fifty thousand, concern trated en masse in a semi-circle of from three to four leagues in extent, and with twelve hundred pieces of cannon. Thus the enemv had constantly fresh troops in reserve, to fill up the gaps caused by our artillerv. " Throughout the fatal dav every hour was marked by a new misfortune þÿ a new loss. The deaths of Generals Vial and Rochambeau were successively announced. The fog, the smoke, and the tumult of the melee scarcely permitted us to recognize each other. We found it very difficult to follow the Emperor. We repeatedly lost sight of him. He was continually moving from place to place, braving the greatest dangers, and disdaining life without victory. ' Hitherto the conflict had been maintained with various chances on both sides. An aidde-camp of General Kegnier arrived. He brought intelligence that the Saxon army and the Wortemberg cavalry under General

Nermann, that is to say, twelve thousand men and forty pieces of artillery, had gone over to Bornadotte 'I he latter had ordered the commander of the Saxon aitillery to turn his guns and fire on the French. For some moments the Emperor sat on his horse as motionless as a statue. He raised his eyes as if appealing to the justice of Heaven. 'Infamous !' he exclaimed. The word was re" peated by a thousand voices. Imprecations and expressions of rage resounded on all sides. Several Saxon officers, who remained faithful to us, broke their swords, and overcome by shame for the baseness of their countrymen, retired to the rear of the army. ' No matter,' said a dragoon of the escort : ' we can do without the cowardly dogs. Your Majesty has still your French army to count upon !' He darted with the rapidity of lightning into the midst of the melee. Shouts of vive Emperor ! Mort aux Saxons ! were echoed from mouth to mouth. All the escort followed the dragoon. The officers alone remained at their post near the Emperor. " A few minutes afterwards a young officer of hussars, whose name I forget, rushed headlong into the enemy's ranks. In a charge some of the miserable renegades had carried off one of our eagles. The gallant young officer rescued it, but it was at the cost of his life. He threw it at the Emperor's feet, and then fell himself, mortally wounded and bathed in his blood. The Emperor was deeply moved by this incident: ' With such men,' said he, ' what resources does France possess!'

" But valour and courage could not overcome destiny. Our ammunition was exhausted before our blood. For the first time we re" tired from the field of battle without bavin" o conquered ; and we commenced that fatal retreat, to which the unfortunate men who had escaped death in the conflict found their

graves in the waters of the Elster. Thus perished Poniatowski, the idol of the brave and devoted Poles. " On the morning of the 19th the Emperor proceeded to the palace of the King of Saxony. The sovereigns took an affectionate leave of each other. The King was inconsolable for the conduct of the Saxon army ; the blush of shame overspread his venerable forehead. The Queen and the Princess Augusta offered the Emperor every assurance of their friendly feeling ; they were alarmed at the dangers to which he was exposed, and with uplifted hands, and eyes streaming with tears, they supplicated him to depart. The King of Saxonv threw himself into Napoleon's arms, calling him his son and his friend, and the Emperor tore himself from the embraces of this excellent family, whose conduct presented a consolatory picture amidst the many examples of royal turpitude ! " Murat separated from the Emperor at. Erfurt, under the pretext that his presence at Naples was indispensable for the defence of his kingdom. At the advanced posts, on the 22d of October, he had stipulated conventions with Austria and England. 1 will not add a word to this fact. Murat expiated his crime by a terrible death I respect his misfortune. " Every day of our retreat mas marked by a new engagement We were doomed to reach France only by marching over the bleeding corpses of our countrymen. At Hanau the Imperial Guard, the precious wreck of our valiant grand army, gained a victory over the combined Bavarian forces,

commanded by General Wrede. This man, too, had armed all the distinction he was possessed of by serving for the space of ten years under the French flag. 'I he Emperor had conferred many favours on Wrede. " On the 2d of November we entered Mentz, and all our troops crossed the Rhine. The Emperor then determined to proceed to Saint Cloud. Only six months had elapsed since we quitted that residence, and in that shoit space of time we had iost ail þÿ even hope ! ! Several days elapsed before we bad an j opportunity of renewing our conversation with the Duke de Vicenza, who was so ill as to be compelled to keep his room. We visited him regularly ; but the restorative which I had formerly employed with success was now no longer at my command. The pleasing recollections of Russia were exhausted, and 1 was, of course, anxious to divert the mind of the invalid from painful reminiscences. But that knowledge of the heart, that exquisite fact with which the Duke de Vicenza was so eminently gifted, enabled him to discern the motives of my reserve. Holding out his hand to me, he said in a tone of kindness, " I observe that your questions have ceased, yet 1 feel assured that your curiosity is not gratified. But I see how it is ; you check your curiosity from feelings of consideration towards me. You are reluctant to call hack my memory to a period to which 1 cannot revert without pain; yet that period is almost constantly present in my thoughts. Profit, therefore, 1 entreat you, by the faint

spark of life which yet animates me, and which will ere long be extinct." "Oh! Duke I" I exclaimed "I entertain no such gloomy anticipations. On our return to Paris I trust we shall frequently have the happiness of enjoying your si ciety ; then your health will be improved, and I shall not hesitate to put your goodness under contribution."

" Now or never." said he sorrowfully. "I feel that my life is fast ebbing away, To me the future has no promise. Grant me but a few days, and then we will resume our favourite subject " " Well !" replied I, with difficulty restraining my tears, " we shall remain at Plombieres until you depart II you continue ill our services are at your command, and if you get better we will take advantage of every fine day to renew our walks and conversations." In mountainous districts ihe autumn is short. Plombieres, which had been so gay and so full of company on my arrival, was now almost deserted. The birds of passage, who had gone thither in quest of health or pleasure, were rapidly taking flight. The season for the waters was past, and we were almost the only visitors remaining in Plombieres : vet how gladly would I have continued there the whole winter through, to hear the Duke de Vicenza describe the stirring events of the Empire There were yet many incidents in the career of Napoleon which I wished to hear authentically related. The last acts of the great drama were of recent occurrence, and yet 1 knew them but superficially. I was, above all, curious to he made acquainted with that striking period in the Emperor's reign, the close of the year 1813, when intrigue and treason were hatched under the very eves of the sovereign, and in the bosom of the capital. Who so well qualified as the Minister for Foreign Affairs to furnish me a key to the odious machinations which so powerfully contributed to overthrow

the imperial government, J wished to accompany the faithful equerry of Napoleon to that said apartment at Fontainebleau, to which the Duke was one among I he few admitted. I wished to follow him to the Palace of the Tuilcries, were, during the Hundred Days, the brilliant hopes with which national enthusiasm had inspired the intrepid deserter from Elba vanished like a dream. þÿ I wished to hear the Duk ; describe the dramatic scenes of Malmaison þÿ that fairy palace, whose gilded saloons and perfumed gardens, once the abode of taste and happiness, became in 1813 the temporary jail of the condemned sovereign. The Duke's health gradually improved, and, after a little time, we resumed our morning excursions and our evening conversations. " Do you recollect at what point I stopped?" said he. þÿ New York Albion.

From the New York American. Extract from Incidents of Travel in Greece, Turkey, Russia, and Poland. " The next day I took a caique at Tophana, and went up to the shipyards at the head of the Golden Horn to visit Mr. Rhodes, to whom I had a letter from a friend in Smyrna. Mr. Rhodes is a native of Long Island, but from his boyhood a resident of this city, and I take great pleasure in saying that lie is an honor to our State and country. The reader will remember that, some years ago, Mr- Eckford, one of our most prominent citizens' under a pressure of public and domestic calamities, left his native city. He sailed from New York in a beautiful corvette, its destination unknown, and came to anchor under the walls of the seraglio in the harbor of Constantinople. The sultan saw her, admired her, and bought her þÿ and I saw her " riding like a tiling of life" on the waters of of the Golden Horn, a model of beauty. The fame of his skill, and the beautiful specimen fie carried out with him, recommended Air Eckford to the Sultan as a fit

Instrument to build up the character of the Ottoman Navy; and afterward, when his full value became known, the Sultan remarked of him, that America must be a great nation if she could spare from her service such a man. Had he lived, even in the decline of life he would have made for himself a reputation in that distant quarter of the globe equal to that he had left behind him, and doubtless would have reaped the attendant precuniary reward. Mr. Rhodes went out as Mr. Eckford's foreman, and on his death the task of completing his employer's work devolved on him. It could not have fallen upon a better man. From a journeyman shipbuilder, all at once Mr Rhodes found himself brought into close relations with the Seraskier Pacha, the Reis K fiend i, the Grand Vizier, and the Sultan himself ; but his good sense never deserted him. lie was then preparing for the launch of the great ship; the longest, as he said, and he new the dimensions of every ship that floated, in the wor'd. I accompanied him over the ship and through the yards, and it was with no small degree of interest that I viewed a townsman, an entire stranger in the country bv his skill alone standing at the head of the great naval establishment of the Sultan. He was dressed in a bine roundabout jacket, without whiskers or mustache, and, except that he wore the tarboueh, was thorough American in his appearance and manners, while his dragoman was constantly by his side, communicating his orders to hundreds of mustached Turks, and in the same breath

be was talking with me of ship builders in New York, and people and things most familiar in our native city. Mr. Rhodes knows and cares but little for things that do not immediately concern him ; his w hole thoughts are of his business, and in that he possesses an ambition and industry worthy of all praise. As an instance of his discretion, particularly proper in the service of that suspicious and despotic government, I may mention that, while standing near the ship and remarking a piece of cloth stretched across her stern, 1 asked him her name, and he told me he did not you know ; that it was painted on her stern, and his dragoman knew, but ho had never looked under, that he might not be able to answer when asked. I have seldom met a countryman abroad with whom I was more pleased, and at parting he put himself on a pinnacle in my estimation, by telling me that, If I came, to the yard the next day at one, 1 would see the Sultan ! There was no man living whom I had a greater curiosity to see. At twelve o'clock I was at the yard, but the Sultan did not come. I went again, and his highness had come two hours before the time: fiad accompanied Mr. Rhodes over the ship, and left the yard less than five minutes before my arrival ; bis caique was still lying at the little dock, his attendants were carrying trays of Tclrcshment to a shooting ground in the rear, and two black eunuchs belonging to the seraglio, handsomely dressed in long black cloaks ol line pelisse cloth, with gold-headed

canes and rings on their fingers, were still lingering about the ship, their effeminate faces and musical voices at once betraying their neutral character. The next was the day of the launch ; and early in the morning, in the suite of Commodore Porter, I went on board an old steamer provided bv the Sultan expressly for the use of Air. Rhodes' American friends. The

®AST3Jt T23TI3T3>33Z m3®3am31T®3 A'TttSwafers of the Golden Horn were already covered- -thousands of caiques, with their high sharp points, were cutting through if, or resting like gulls upon its surface ; and there were ships with the still proud banner of the cresent, and strangers with the flags of every nation in Christendom, and sail boats, longboats, and row-boats, ambassador's barges, and caiques of eflendis, beys and pachas with red silk flags streaming in the wind, while countless thousands were assembled on the banks to behold the extraordinary spectacle of an American ship, the largest in the world, launched in the harbor of old Stamboul The Sultan was then living at his beautiful palace at Sweet Waters, and was obliged to pass by our boat ; he had made a great affair of the launch ; had invited all the diplomatic corps, and, through the Reis Eflendi, particularly requested the presence of Commodore Porter ; had stationed his harem on the opposite side of the river, and, as I saw, prepared for himself near the ship a tent of scarlet cloth trimmed with gold I expected to see him appear in all the pomp and splendor of the greatest potentate on earth. I had already seen enough to convince me that the days of Eastern magnificence had gone by, or that the gorgeous scenes which my imagination had always connected with the East had never existed ; but still I could not divest myself of the lingering idea of the power and splendor ol the Sultan. þÿ His commanding style to his own subjects: "1 command you, , my

slave, that you bring the head of , my slave, and lay it at my feet;'' and then his lofty tone with foreign powers : " I. who am, by the infinate grace of the great, just, and all powerful Creator, and the abundance of the miracles of the chief of his prophets, emperor of powerful emperors ; refuge of sovereigns, distributer of crowns to the kings of the earth ; keeper of the two very holy cities (Mecca and Medina) ; governor of the holy city of Jerusalem ; master of Europe, Asia and Africa, conquered with our victorious sword and our terrible lance ; lord of two seas (Black and White); of Damascus, the odor of Paradise ; of Bagdad, the seat of the califs, of the fortresses of Belgrade, Agra, and a multitude of countries, isles, straits, people, generations, and of so many victorious armies who repose under the shade of our Sublime Porte. 1, in shoit, who am the shadow of God upon earth." þÿ 1 was rolling these things through my mind when a murmur. " The Sultan is coming," turned me to the side of the boat, and one view dispelled all my gorgeous fancies. There was no style, no state ; a citizen king, a republican president, or a democratic governor, could not have made a more unpretending appearance than did this " shadow of God upon earth " He was seated in the bottom of a plain caique dressed in the military frock-coat and red tarbouoh, with his long black heard, the only mark of a Turk about him, and he moved slowly along the vacant space cleared for his passage, boats with the flags of every

nation, and thousands of caiques falling back, and the eyes of the immense multitude earnestly fixed upon him, hut without any shouts or acclamations ; and when he landed at the little dock, and his great officers bowed to the dust before him, he looked the plainest, mildest, kindest man among them. 1 had wished to see him as a wholesale mnrdercr, who had more blood upon hi hand than any

man livtng; who bad slaughtered the Janissaries, drencod the plains of Greece, to say nothing of bastinadoes, impalements, cutting off heads, and tying up in sacks, which ate taking place every momeni ; hut I will not believe that Sultan Mahmond finds any pleasure in shedding blood. J)ire necessity, or> as he himself would see, fate, has ever been driving liirn on I look upon him as one of the most interesting characters upon earth ; as the creature of circumstances, made bloody & cruel by the necessities of his position. I look at his past life, and at that which is yet in store for him, through all the stormy scenes he is to pass until he completes his unhappy destiny þÿ the last of a powerful and once-dreaded race, bearded by those who once crouched at the footstool of his ancestors, goaded by rebellious vassals, conscious that he is going a downward road, and yet unable to resist the impulse that drives In'm on. Like the strong man encompassed with a net, he finds no avenue of escape, and cannot break through it. The Seraskier Pacha & other public officers escorted him to his tent, and now all the interest which 1 had taken in the Sultan was transferred to Mr. Rhodes. He had great axniety about the launch, and many difficulties to contend with; first, in the Turks' jealously of a stranger, which obliged him to keep constantly on the watch, lest some of the ropes should be cut or fastenings knocked away: and he had another Turkish prejudice to struggle against þÿ the day had been fixed

twice before, but the astronomers found an unfortunate conjunction of the stars, and it was postponed, and even then the stars were unpropitious ; but Mr. Rhodes insisted that the work had gone so far that it could riot be stopped. And besides these, he had another difficulty, in his ignorance of their language. With more than a thousand men under htm, all his orders had to pass through interpreters, and often, too, the most prompt action was necessary, and the least mistake might prove fatal. Fortunately, he was protected from treachery by the kindness of Mr. Churchill and Dr, Zohrab, one of whom stood on the how and the other in the stern of the ship, and through whom every order was transmitted in Turkish. Probably none there fell the same interest that we did ; for the flags of the barbarian and every nation in Christens dom were waving around us. and at that distance from home the enterprise of a single citizen enlisted the warmest feelings of every American We watched the ship with as keen an intcresi as if our own honor and success depended upon her movements. For a long time she remained perfectly quiet. At length she moved, slowly and almost imperceptibly; and then, as if conscious that the eyes of an immense multitude were on her, that the honor of a distant nation was in some measure at stake, she marched proudly to the water, plunged in with a force that almost buried her, and, rising like a hug© leviathan, parted the foaming waves with her how, and rode triumphantly upon them-

Even .Mussulman indifference was disturbed ; all petty jealousies were hitshpd ; the whole immense mass roused into admiration ; loud and long continued shouts of applause ros© with one accord from Turks and Christians, ami the Sultan was so transported that h© jumped up and trapped his hands like a school- boy. Mr. Rhodes' triumph was complete j Ik© Saltan called l ire tv «r» leal,

From the London Times August 15, 1838. j Tun Birmingham Meeting þÿ We were ; purposely silent in our last publication on the renewed attempt to congregate the operative classes of this district, as we were unwilling to add to the delusion bv the importance and publicity a notice of this kind would have afforded it. It was easy to observe from the provincial newspapers that failures had already taken place in other districts, notwithstanding the statements that had been made weekly on the subject and the sedulous efforts exhibited in the columns of our contemporary for some time past. We observe, however, the most 'ridiculous statements on this

point in some of the London prints : they appear to have multiplied the real number of attendants by ten. The whole scene was rather that of a wake or holyday, such as "Saint Monday" would be likely to present, and as an expression of popular feeling it must, without doubt, be viewed as a total failure. The truth of the matter is, that there is more contentment manifested by our operative classes, and that we hope arising from increased employment, than is consistent with their listening to the extravagant attempts of political agitators to unsettle the constitution of the kingdom as fixed by the Reform Bill, and thus to sultifv themselves as to all that had previously engaged their anxious efforts.-- Birmingham Gazette.

Hanover. þÿ The opinion gains ground in Germany that the Diet must interfere in the affairs of Hanover. The deputies of opposition, previous to the prorogation, are known to have addressed a petition to the Diet, which is thus legally called on to interfere. Prussia, which at one time warmly supported King Ernest, has fallen off from him. The conduct of the latter at Berlin lately was highly displeasing to the Prussian monarch and ministers, and the prospect of a speedy settlement of the quarrel caused by the arrest of the Archbishop of Cologne relieves Prussia of being too obsequious to his mad Majesty of Hanover.

The American and British flags flaunted at her masts on Saturday, The interior of the vessel is equally wonderful þÿ it is like a little town, there being two fiats of berths, which amount, we are given to understand, to 300. March of Invention. þÿ Steam Music þÿ Amongst the numerous inventions which almost daily claim a share of public attention, we have to notice that of a steam organ, invented and adapted to the " Tyne" locomotive engine, the property of the Newcastle and Carlisle Railway Company, by ihe Rev. James Birkett, ofOvinghaai. As far as we are able to judge, this instrument bears the greatest resemblance to the organ. It consists of eight pipes turned to compass, what is termed by musicians, an octave, but without any intervening tones of semitones. This is the first attempt to adapt a musical instrument, to the steam engine capable ol producing a tune, and, though not so perfect as to admit of all the pleasing variety and combination of sounds as the instrument to which we have compared it, there is no doubt but very considerable improvements will be made in tins steam musical instrument by the inventor, who is a skilful musician as well as an ingenious mechanic. Wc understood that some important alterations are at present in progress, and intended to be completed previous to the grand opening of the railway on the 18 August. þÿ Tyne Mercury. From the New York Albion, Sept. 29, 1838. By the Great Western we are in possession of London papers to the 7th inst. Parliament was prorogued by the Queen in person on the 16 ult., when her Majesty gave her assent to several bills The deportment ot the roval fair one was most dignified And she read her speech in a clear and impressive manner. At those passages which had particular reference to the prosperity of the nation, and the happiness of her people, her Majesty was very emphatic. T he cause of the Spanish Carlisls is again triumphant ; the troops of Carlos have gained a splendid victory. What the subsequent events may be we cannot pretend to say.

Canada. þÿ The accounts frotn the Lower Province represent the public mind as undergoing much excitement in consequence of the proceedings in England with regaid to the Earl of Durham. Ma rtv openly condemn the whole transaction, and all seem to regret its occurrence. In Montreal, it is purposed by the Herald and other journals, to call a public meeting in his behalf, asked his lordship not to resign his high office. We doubt however, if he will listen to these solicitations, as he doubtless feels himself offended at what has taken place at home generally, and with the cowardly way in which lie was thrown over by Lord Melbourne particularly. At a recent interview with the gentlemen, deputies from the Lower Provinces, for the purpose of framing the plan of a Federal Lrnion, his lordship gave vent to his feelings on this point very emphatically ; he was indeed so much overcome as to be obliged to retire for a few minutes to another part of the room He is determined on retracing his steps to England without delay, and will take his departure it is presumed about the 10th of October. It is supposed, we know not upon what authority, that his lordship will take the route of Newh ork, where undoubtedly much public attention would be paid him.

Perhaps i here can be no greater recommendation of the qualities of this vessel, than the consideration of the earnestness with which passengers crowd to cross the Atlantic in her Alfeady upwards of one hundred berths are taken, for the outward voyage, and she is actually bespoke in full for her next trip from Bristol. Steam Navigation may now be considered as fully established, and its convenience are every day more and more appreciated.

Lower Canada. þÿ The murderers of Chartrand have been acquitted, notwithstanding the most irrefragable evidence was produced of their guilt ; in fact, no denial of the murderous act was attempted, and the counsel for the accused almost put in a plea of justification. We have given a short abstract of the proceedings, by which the reader will see how farcical a thing is a trial by jury in Lower Canada, when a rebel or a murderer is the subject of it. The doctrine of Mr. Mondelet is this þÿ " It is true my friends, the prisoners at the bar have committed murder; but it was not a common murder þÿ it was a political murder, and consequently their offence is merged in the more general one of treason. Now, Lord Durham Iras, by royal proclamation, set all the traitors at liberty, or visited them with only nominal punishment þÿ therefore, you arc bound to follow the same course with the prisoners before you, because it is all the same whether you shoot the Queen's troops in action, or tie Chartrand to a tree and shoot him there!" Upon this ground, it would seem, these atrocious villains were acquitted, and arc now ut large and j doubtless ready to perpetrate the same crimes t

whenever a favourable Opportunity present itself. The Court charged the jury to find the prisoners guilty, but tbev, in defiance of all reason and justice, not only returned a verdict of acquittal, but prenounccd the words " not guilty" in one loud and unanimous shout ! A cheer was then attempted to be got up in the Court House. Chartrand appears to have been a very good and inoffensive person, and drew upon himself the malice of the murderers because he was a loyal subject He had given bis rebel countrymen no offence whatever, be. yond a refusal to enter their traitorous schemes. His brother was in Court during the trial, and appeared to be laboring under an intensity of grief and fraternal affection. Jalbert, the principal person engaged in the murder of Lt Wier of the 32d Regiment, has not been brought to trial, in consequence of the principal witness having been bribed to abscond Jalbert will probably escape the gallows also. These events have filled the minds of the loyal people with alarm. They show that no man is safe in the career of assassination but the assassin himself, since it seems impossible, if be be a Frenchman, to find a jury of his countrymen to convict him. But how long are things to go on in this way '! What does Lord Durham think of the healing elfects of the amnesty now ? Is he still under the delusive hope that such persons can be reconciliated ? If so, then it is time for every loyal man to flee the country, or to take up arms in his own defence, with-

out reference to the Queen's Government at all. Lord Gosford drained the cup of conciliation to the dregs, hut Lord Durham has swallowed dregs and all. Is it possible that his Lordship can much longer hold out under this sad hallucination, especially when he sees all generosity is thrown awav, and that all his acts of magnamity and humanity are ascribed to fear? Wc shall see.- þÿ New York Albion.
